title: Some Silly Inventions That Became Wildly Popular
summary: Josh and Chuck count down silly direct response TV inventions that became popular, opening with George Foreman grill as a non-silly example of the genre. Covered: the Thigh Master (Suzanne Summers pitching a Swedish physical therapist's V bar), Ron Popeil and his pitches (Vegematic, Inside the Eggshell Scrambler, GLH hair spray), the Pocket Fisherman, the Shake Weight and its sexual innuendo, Big Mouth Billy Bass, the Bedazzler and its Y2K fashion comeback, the Flowbee vacuum haircut attachment invented by Rick Hunts, and the Snuggie blanket with sleeves. Ends with an Instagram comment from a listener about the Kentucky Meat Shower and a social media plug.

segments.title: Intro and George Foreman grill
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on silly direct response TV inventions and explain direct response marketing. They note the George Foreman grill as a non-silly top seller, which Foreman endorsed for a share of profits.

segments.title: Thigh Master
segments.summary: The Thigh Master, originally the V bar invented by Swedish physical therapist Anne Marie Binstrom, was pitched by Suzanne Summers in 1991 ads with a doctor in a lab coat. Summers later bought out partners and reportedly earned large sums; she was inducted into the Direct Response Hall of Fame in 2014.

segments.title: Ron Popeil and the Pocket Fisherman
segments.summary: Ron Popeil's career as an infomercial pioneer, starting with the Vegematic, plus his Inside the Eggshell Scrambler and GLH hair product. Then the Pocket Fisherman, a compact folding fishing rod sold by Ronco.

segments.title: Transition to Shake Weight
segments.summary: Brief transition to the next item on the list.

segments.title: Shake Weight
segments.summary: The Shake Weight, a spring-loaded dumbbell-like workout device popular largely for its sexual innuendo; the makers' studies claimed more muscle activity than traditional dumbbells, and it was widely parodied.

segments.title: Big Mouth Billy Bass
segments.summary: The singing mounted fish invented by Joe Peltier, inspired by his wife Barbara's suggestion at a Bass Pro Shop. It sold around one hundred million dollars worth in about a year, spread by word of mouth, and was later knocked off with other songs.

segments.title: Bedazzler
segments.summary: The Bedazzler rhinestone setting tool, first called the Stud Setter and Ronco Rhinestone, invented by Herman Brickman, a protege of Ron Popeil. It became a fashion trend in the nineties and a Y2K-era craze, with a modern revival in crafts.

segments.title: Bedazzler revival
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how bedazzling has returned as a tedious, meditative craft applied to objects like phone cases and jars.

segments.title: Flowbee
segments.summary: The Flowbee, a vacuum attachment for home haircuts invented by California cabinet carpenter Rick Hunts, who sold his business to fund it. He promoted it with a thirty-minute fake infomercial hosted by Lenny McGill, selling around two million units. George Clooney reportedly uses it.

segments.title: Snuggie
segments.summary: The Snuggie, a blanket with sleeves that sold around twenty-five million units from 2008 to about 2013. Predecessors included the Slanket and other blankets with sleeves.

segments.title: Instagram comment on Kentucky Meat Shower
segments.summary: A listener comment from Instagram about the Kentucky Meat Shower short stuff episode, asking whether the hosts love Kentucky. The hosts discuss other Kentucky episodes and ask for show location suggestions.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts plug social media and email contact, and sign off with production credit.
